item.title: Research explores the development and evaluation of in-context learning in language models
item.description:
Research explores the development and evaluation of in-context learning in language models

A study titled “From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning,” submitted on 13 October 2026, investigates how language models acquire and improve the ability to adapt behavior based on prompts. The research indicates that in-context learning (ICL) does not develop as a uniform capability but follows distinct trajectories for prompt control, answer preference, and composition.

🔍 Overview

Researchers utilized a controlled diagnostic to distinguish between models that simply copy nearby demonstrations and those that integrate information across a prompt. Results across 17 models show:

  • Approximately one-third prefer the copied answer.
  • A small number of models remain undecided.
  • The remainder favor rule-consistent answers, which correlates with higher accuracy.

🧩 How it works

Checkpoint analyses reveal that models begin prioritizing task-relevant tokens over conflicting examples long before their overall accuracy improves beyond chance. The research also explored training methods to influence these behaviors:

  • Synthetic documents defining endings shift models toward compositional responses.
  • Fine-tuning on definition exercises improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings.

💡 Why it matters

The study suggests that evaluation setups for ICL are complex. Investigators identified 8 aspects, such as task formulation and the number of in-context examples, to better measure model performance. Their findings yield concrete recommendations:

Recommendation Observation
Multiple Prompts Consistently useful across models
Task Formulation Depends on model scale

Furthermore, the research confirms that gain over “no document” baselines does not necessarily establish that a model requires specific passage retrieval, highlighting the need for precise comparison models and conditions in future evaluations.

#MachineLearning #LanguageModels #InContextLearning #AIResearch

item.title: Study Evaluates Retrieval-Based In-Context Learning for Detecting Defamatory Hate Speech
item.description:
Study Evaluates Retrieval-Based In-Context Learning for Detecting Defamatory Hate Speech

With hate speech pervasive online, automatic detection of criminally relevant posts is essential. A new study examines retrieval‑based in‑context learning (RetICL) strategies for detecting defamatory offences under §§185‑187 StGB, the focus of GermEval 2026 Subtask 4.

🔍 Overview

  • Hate speech is ubiquitous online; automatic detection is crucial for criminally relevant social‑media posts.
  • The research targets defamatory offences defined in §§185‑187 StGB as part of GermEval 2026 Subtask 4.

🧩 Approach

  • Evaluated a variety of retrieval‑based in‑context learning (RetICL) strategies.
  • Compared prompting styles: zero‑shot, few‑shot, retrieval‑based demonstrations, and an optimized static set of demonstrations.
  • Incorporated concrete legal knowledge into the inputs.

⚙️ Findings

  • Few‑shot prompting beats zero‑shot.
  • Retrieval‑based approaches provide only marginal gains over random demonstrations and fall behind an optimized static set of demonstrations.
  • Supplying concrete legal knowledge helps, yet the choice of model outweighs every other system choice.
  • Models over‑predict criminal relevance while missing 26‑57 % of criminally relevant posts, making them more suitable for triage rather than autonomous moderation.
Prompting Strategy Relative Performance
Zero‑shot Baseline
Few‑shot Beats zero‑shot
Retrieval‑based (random demos) Marginal gain over zero‑shot
Optimized static demos Outperforms retrieval‑based

💡 Why it matters

  • Automatic detection is vital given the prevalence of hate speech online.
  • Recognizing the current models’ tendency to over‑predict and miss a substantial share of relevant posts guides realistic expectations for their role in legal moderation pipelines.

#AI #HateSpeechDetection #InContextLearning #LegalAI

Source: MUCnoHARM@GermEval Shared Task 2026: Retrieval-based In-Context Learning for Defamatory Offences, and Where It Falls Short
